# agent-kit catalog

## essentials 0.2.0

Everyday engineering skills that work in any agent, for commit messages, cross-tool session handoffs, grilling a plan before you act on it, and sharpening a task to be deeper instead of bigger.

- `commit-message`: Write a clear git commit message (Conventional Commits style) from the staged diff. Use when the user asks to commit, write or improve a commit message, or summarize staged changes for a commit.
- `grilling`: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- `handoff-notes`: Write a concise handoff note so another agent session, another tool (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, pi, OpenCode), or a teammate can resume the current work without re-reading the conversation. Use when the user says hand off, wrap up, save progress, pause, switch tools, or before a context reset.
- `sharpen`: Make a task deeper, not bigger, then rewrite the prompt. Use for /sharpen.

## eng-leadership 0.1.0

Skills for engineering leaders, for design/RFC reviews and structured interview kits.

- `design-review`: Review a technical design doc, RFC, or ADR the way a senior engineering leader would - find risks, gaps, and unclear decisions, and give prioritized, actionable feedback. Use when asked to review, critique, or poke holes in a design, RFC, proposal, architecture doc, or ADR.
- `interview-kit`: Build a structured interview kit for an engineering role - competencies, an interview loop, questions with follow-ups, and a scoring rubric with behavioral anchors. Use when planning hiring for a role, designing an interview loop, writing interview questions, or creating a scorecard or rubric.

## research-tools 0.1.0

Up-to-date library and API documentation lookup via the Context7 MCP server, with a no-MCP fallback.

- `library-docs`: Look up current, version-specific documentation and code examples for a library, framework, SDK, or API before writing or fixing code that uses it. Use when working with a third-party package, when an API may have changed, when unsure of a function signature, or when the user asks for up-to-date docs.
- MCP servers: `context7`

## principles 0.2.0

Twenty-four named engineering principles (prove it works, fix root causes, subtract before you add, build the lever, and more) that steer how agents design, build and verify, plus a benchmark checklist. One skill with one file per principle.

- `principles`: Named engineering principles (prove it works, fix root causes, subtract before you add, build the lever, and 20 more) that steer how an agent designs, builds and verifies. Use when a task or the user names a principle, when beau-mode tells you to apply one, or when deciding how much to build, where state and validation live, or what counts as proof.

## bstack 0.7.0

Beau's rigorous agent workflow. beau-mode routes each task to a playbook and the principles; beau-help lists what the kit can do and what's new; skills for understanding (how, why, teach, recall), proof (verify-work, create- and maintain-verification-skill, create- and maintain-formal-verification-skill, swarm), design and planning (architect, arena, state-machines, technical-writing), product repos (scaffold-product and the Product phase playbook), review and trails (interrogate, show-me-your-work), and improvement (reflect, correct, unslop) do the steps. Adapted from Lauren Tan's pstack to work in any agent.

- `architect`: Design before code. Ground in the affected systems, sketch types and signatures in at least two structurally different shapes (via arena), pick one, implement against it, and scrap it when friction shows the shape is wrong. Use for /architect, "design this", or work where jumping to code would lock in the wrong shape.
- `arena`: Run N parallel candidates at the same task (ideally on different models), have a judge on another model score them against a rubric, pick a base, and graft the best parts of the others into it. Use for /arena, "arena this", "throw it in the arena", or when one attempt at a non-trivial artifact (a design, an API, a doc, a tricky function) would lock in the wrong shape.
- `beau-help`: List what agent-kit and bstack can do (skills, playbooks, subagents) and how to call each one, or show what changed since you last looked. Use for /beau-help, "what can you do", "which skill should I use for X", "what's new", or "what changed in bstack".
- `beau-mode`: Beau's way of doing engineering work with an agent. It picks a playbook, applies named principles, verifies on the real artifact, keeps a decision trail, and writes plain replies. Use for /beau-mode, "beau mode", or any non-trivial engineering task (a bug, a feature, a refactor, a perf problem, an investigation, a prototype, a skill edit, or an unattended run). Skip it for casual questions and one-line answers.
  - playbook **Authoring a skill** (`playbooks/authoring-a-skill.md`). Writing or editing a SKILL.md, a playbook, or a principle.
  - playbook **Autonomous run** (`playbooks/autonomous-run.md`). A long task to drive to completion without stopping: "run until done", "going to bed", "don't ask me".
  - playbook **Bug fix** (`playbooks/bug-fix.md`). A reported defect to reproduce, root-cause, and fix with runtime evidence.
  - playbook **Eval** (`playbooks/eval.md`). Testing how a skill, principle or prompt change affects agent behavior before you keep it, including adopting someone else's skill.
  - playbook **Feature** (`playbooks/feature.md`). New or changed behavior, built from a named data shape.
  - playbook **Investigation** (`playbooks/investigation.md`). A read-only question: how does X work, why was Y built this way, are we sure about Z, should we do X or Y.
  - playbook **Multi-phase plan** (`playbooks/multi-phase-plan.md`). Turning an agreed design into a tactical execution plan of small, verifiable PRs: "turn this design into a plan", a migration, or any change too big for one PR.
  - playbook **Opening a PR** (`playbooks/opening-a-pr.md`). The last step of every playbook that changes code.
  - playbook **Pause safely** (`playbooks/pause-safely.md`). An explicit request to pause, going offline, a restart, or imminent context compaction. Never on "keep going".
  - playbook **Perf issue** (`playbooks/perf-issue.md`). A measured slowness to trace and improve against a baseline.
  - playbook **Product phase** (`playbooks/product-phase.md`). Product work in a repo with docs/VISION.md and docs/phases/: specifying the next phase, advancing one, or closing it at its gate. Also the entry point for starting a product.
  - playbook **Prototype** (`playbooks/prototype.md`). A throwaway sketch to make a design or behavior decision cheaply, or to settle a factual question by observing it instead of asking.
  - playbook **Refactoring** (`playbooks/refactoring.md`). A behavior-preserving change to structure: rename, extract, inline, dedupe, move, reshape an API.
  - playbook **Session pickup** (`playbooks/session-pickup.md`). Resuming or taking over another agent's in-flight work from a transcript, a handoff note, or a pushed branch.
- `correct`: Find the mistakes agents keep repeating in this repo and make each one impossible. Tries architecture first, then types, then a lint or CI check whose error names the fix, then a test, and docs last, and proves each new check fails on a real past mistake. Use for /correct, "agents keep doing X", or after correcting the same mistake twice.
- `create-formal-verification-skill`: Generate a project-local verify-AREA skill that formally verifies the code where a bug costs the most and tests reach the least, in any language, with whichever verification tool fits (model checker, prover, SMT-backed verifier). Use for /create-formal-verification-skill, "model-check this race", "prove this invariant", or when concurrency, retries, state machines, parsers or unsafe code need more than tests.
- `create-verification-skill`: Generate a project-local verify-APP skill (for example verify-curator) that launches the real app, drives it like a user through a control CLI, captures evidence, and keeps a feature map. Any stack or surface. Use for /create-verification-skill, "make a control skill for this repo", or when a project has no scripted way to prove behavior.
- `figure-it-out`: Design a rigorous, auditable playbook for work no standard playbook fits (a large migration, an ambitious multi-part change, or anything the human will review after stepping away), then run it as a hypothesis loop with a decision trail. Use for "figure it out", large or cross-cutting changes, or overnight and unattended work.
- `how`: Explain how a subsystem, feature or code path works, at the level a senior engineer needs before changing it, covering runtime flow, key concepts, where things live and gotchas. Use for "how does X work", walkthroughs before a change, onboarding to unfamiliar code, and "where should this live" or "which layer owns this" questions.
- `interrogate`: Adversarial multi-model review of a diff, branch, PR or design. Several adversaries try to break it, and a finding survives only when a run proves it. Use for "interrogate", "adversarial review", "tear this apart", "stress test this change", "find blind spots", or before shipping a contested or risky change.
- `maintain-formal-verification-skill`: Bring a project's formal verification back in line with the code after the code changes. Finds the commits that touched verified code, updates the model, harness or properties to describe the code as it is now, reruns, and says whether each failure is drift in the verification or a bug in the code. Use for /maintain-formal-verification-skill, "is the model still true to the code", or after merges and refactors that touched verified code without rechecking it.
- `maintain-verification-skill`: Periodic pass that keeps a project's verification skill and feature map honest. Read-only subagents check each feature against source, one live session drives every feature, and at most one PR ships proven corrections. Use for /maintain-verification-skill, "audit the verify skill", "is the feature map still right", or as a daily scheduled task.
- `recall`: Rebuild the user's recent context on a topic from their own agent transcripts, the PRs, tickets and reports around it, and live git state, then return a short brief and the next move. Use for "recall my work on X", "catch me up on X", "where did I leave off", before starting or resuming work.
- `reflect`: Mine the current session for durable lessons and turn each one into a concrete, approved edit to a skill, playbook or principle, or a backlog item. Three independent reviewers read the transcript, a synthesizer sorts their findings, and nothing changes without the user's approval. Use when the user says reflect, "capture what we learned", or "so the next run doesn't repeat this".
- `scaffold-product`: Set up a repo for product work with agents, either a new product or an existing repo that predates this workflow. Writes the vision, decision log, phase specs, roadmap and agent instructions, then creates its verification skill, and checks the result with check-product.py. Use for "start a new product", "scaffold this repo", "adopt this repo into beau-mode", or when beau-mode's Product phase playbook finds no docs/VISION.md.
- `show-me-your-work`: Keep a reviewable decision trail for long, unattended or multi-phase work (one TSV row per decision with what, why, evidence and result), then audit it against the transcript and have a different model flag what deserves attention. Use for /show-me-your-work, "keep a decision log", autonomous or overnight runs, or "catch me up on what you did".
- `state-machines`: Find the implicit state machines in a codebase (lifecycles spread across booleans, status strings, nullable fields, effects and handlers), show which states conflict with exact lines, then make them explicit as a checked spec and a pure transition function with IO at the edge. Use for "find all the implicit state machines in my app", "which states can conflict", "make this state explicit", "model this as a state machine", "review this state machine", or before an agent builds anything with a lifecycle (loading/error, forms, modals, auth, checkout, uploads, jobs, sync, agent loops).
- `swarm`: Fan out N parallel workers (local subagents, or cloud agents where your tool has them), wait for all of them, and return one consolidated report. Use for /swarm, "swarm this", parallel coverage of many slices, races of N attempts at one brief, live-verification lanes, fuzzing, or collecting enough perf samples to trust a number.
- `teach`: Explain a body of work plainly so a person actually understands it, by running the how and why skills and weaving what they find into one clear, layered explanation with diagrams that build up step by step. Use for "teach me this", "help me really understand X", "explain this change or subsystem to me", or "prove to me this approach is better".
- `technical-writing`: Layered technical-writing standard (Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, Simplified Technical English instruction rules, Global English syntax). Use for /technical-writing, README-driven planning, or when writing or reviewing docs, READMEs, RFCs, design docs, plans, PR descriptions or commit messages.
- `unslop`: Cut AI writing tells from prose, such as filler, inflated vocabulary, em dashes, rule-of-three padding, chatbot phrases, vague metaphors, over-compression. Use when writing or reviewing any prose (replies, docs, READMEs, PR descriptions, commit messages, skill files), or when asked to unslop, tighten or de-AI text.
- `verify-work`: Prove a change works by checking the real artifact (run the feature, read the actual value, drive the real surface) and return VERIFIED, NOT VERIFIED or INCONCLUSIVE with evidence. Use before saying any task is done, when asked "does it work", "prove it", "verify", or when a claim rests on "it compiles" or "tests pass".
- `why`: Find out why code is the way it is (design rationale, past decisions, regressions, where a threshold came from) by searching git, PRs and every connected ticket, doc, chat and observability tool in parallel, and return a cited, confidence-tiered answer. Use for "why does X work this way" or "why did we pick Y". Use how for what code does.
- subagent `beau-agent` (Claude Code)

## cfo 0.1.0

A CFO for AI and cloud spending. Keeps a private cost ledger from receipts and provider billing data, separates cash cost from API-equivalent cost, estimates runs before they start, writes a weekly brief, and proposes budgets and cuts for you to approve. Never pays, cancels or deletes anything itself.

- `cfo-books`: Check, append to and summarize the CFO's private books (ledger, projects, budgets, renewals, questions). Checks find schema errors, forbidden content such as card numbers, account IDs and API keys, and rewritten ledger history. Use before committing or opening a PR against the books, to add ledger rows, to get a month's spend numbers, when a books CI check fails, or when asked to "check the books", "validate the ledger" or "summarize the month".
- `cfo-brief`: The CFO's weekly routine. Collects new receipts, invoices, vendor notices and billing data into the private books, checks spend against the budget, finds waste and renewals, writes a brief, and sends it with decisions and questions for the user to approve. Proposes; never acts. Use for "CFO brief", "weekly finance review", "check my spending this week", or from a weekly scheduled task.
- `estimate-run`: Estimate what an agent run, a charter or a whole project will cost before it starts, in both cash and API-equivalent terms, with a typical and a high figure based on past runs where the books have them. Fills a run charter's estimate and budget. Use for "what will this cost", "estimate this run", "price this charter", "is this worth running", or when writing a run charter.
- `spend-snapshot`: Answer "what am I spending" on AI, cloud and developer tools, by provider and by project, with month-to-date spend against the budget, renewals coming up, and anything unknown. Reads the private books plus receipts and billing data from connected tools. Use for "what am I spending", "how much do my AI tools cost", "am I over budget", "spend snapshot", or before deciding on a new tool or plan.
